items.title: 13.1 Volatility of chlorine, bromine and iodine

source_refs.note: Topic 13.1 with the Interesting Information box on bromine, printed page 293. The print's 'chlorine being a liquid' is noted.

blocks.text: Chlorine is very volatile at room temperature and disperses quickly in the air (the print calls it a liquid; it is a gas). Bromine, a liquid, is less volatile than chlorine but more volatile than iodine; it evaporates readily, releasing toxic fumes at room temperature, with an orange vapour and a strong, unpleasant smell (its name comes from the Greek 'bromos', stench). Iodine is the least volatile of the three: at room temperature its solid state shows lower volatility than chlorine and bromine. Volatility therefore decreases from chlorine to iodine, because of the increasing molecular mass, the larger outer shell and the stronger intermolecular (London dispersion) forces down the group.

blocks.caption: Volatility of the three halogens
rows: intermediate; evaporates readily with toxic orange fumes

blocks.prompt: Why is chlorine more volatile than bromine and iodine (Quick Check 13.1c)?
blocks.explanation: Chlorine molecules are the smallest and lightest of the three, with the fewest electrons, so the instantaneous dipole-induced dipole forces between them are weakest; little energy is needed to separate the molecules, and chlorine is a gas that disperses at once, whereas bromine is a liquid and iodine a solid.

items: Volatility Cl2 greater than Br2 greater than I2: it falls with increasing molecular mass, size and London dispersion forces down the group.
